hints: Remember that starch is not one molecule, it is a mixture of amylose and amylopectin. Ask yourself which of those is branched and which is not.
Compare the building blocks: both glycogen and starch are made from alpha-glucose joined by 1,4 and 1,6 glycosidic bonds, so the real difference must be in the amount of branching.
walkthrough:
**Recall what starch really is**

Think of starch as a mixture found in plants. It has amylose, which is unbranched, and amylopectin, which is branched.

Glycogen is the animal store found in liver and muscle. So we need a feature true for all glycogen but not true for all starch.

**Check the similarities first**

Both glycogen and starch are polysaccharides. Both are built only from $\alpha$-glucose monomers.

Both also use the same bonds: $1,4$-glycosidic bonds in the straight chains and $1,6$-glycosidic bonds at branch points. So B, C and D cannot be distinguishing features.

**Spot the branching difference**

Every glycogen molecule is highly branched, with many short side chains close together. This allows very fast hydrolysis for quick energy release.

In starch, only amylopectin is branched (and less highly than glycogen), while amylose has no branches at all. So high branching in every molecule is unique to glycogen, answer A.

options.A: Correct. All glycogen molecules are highly branched, while starch contains unbranched amylose plus less branched amylopectin.
options.B: Both glycogen and starch are polysaccharides, so this is a similarity, not a distinguishing feature.
options.C: Both glycogen and starch (amylose and amylopectin) are made only from alpha-glucose, so this does not distinguish them.
options.D: Both glycogen and starch contain 1,4-glycosidic bonds in their main chains, so this is shared, not distinctive.
